title: From code to a running program
summary: A CPU only runs machine code. Compiled languages translate once, interpreted ones read your code each time: what that changes for errors and for what you install.

scheme: you can read it                the CPU runs it
text: Which language for which job? Glue scripts: often Python or bash. Kernels, drivers, fast servers: C or Rust. The reason is how each one reaches the CPU.
A CPU only understands machine code: numbers that stand for its tiny instructions.
- You write source code, text a person can read.
- A compiler (gcc for C, rustc through cargo for Rust) translates it once into a program file the CPU can run.

scheme: the interpreter reads it on the spot
alone, as many times as you like
text: Python and bash work differently: an interpreter reads your code and runs it on the spot, every time.
- Nothing to build, quick to change and try again.
- But the interpreter must be installed wherever the script runs.

scheme: a misspelled name in a rare branch
C, Rust      the compiler refuses to build:
Python, bash found only when that line runs,
text: It changes when you meet your mistakes.
- A compiler reads the whole file first and catches many mistakes before anything runs: read its messages, they name the file and the line.
- Python checks the grammar of the whole file before it starts, but looks up a name only when its line runs.
- Neither catches wrong logic: test your program in every language, and every branch of a script.

scheme: a C or Rust program   the same CPU and system
a Python script       python3 and its libraries
text: It also changes what you hand over.
- A compiled program is built for one kind of machine, and often needs that system's libraries: build again for another one.
- A script runs anywhere its interpreter and libraries are.
